title: Polymer clay kaleidoscope cane earrings
subtitle: Geometric cane slices on ear studs with a six-fold repeating pattern
excerpt: A kaleidoscope cane is built by assembling triangular colour segments into a hexagonal log, then reducing the log and slicing it to reveal the repeating pattern. Each slice becomes an earring face. The pattern looks complex but is built from five straight-forward steps.
sourceNotes: Millefiori-derived cane technique adapted for kaleidoscope geometry. Technique derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: A PVC-based modelling clay that cures hard in a domestic oven at 110-130°C; decorative, not food-safe
A log of polymer clay with an internal pattern that is visible in cross-section when sliced; the pattern repeats at every slice
Rolling and compressing a cane log to make it longer and narrower while preserving the internal pattern
Kneading polymer clay by hand until warm and pliable before working

content.text: A kaleidoscope
cane
in
polymer clay
is a hexagonal log built from six identical colour-block triangles arranged around a central core. When
reduced
and sliced, the cross-section shows a six-pointed repeating design. Two slices become the faces of a pair of stud earrings.

materials.name: Ear stud blanks with flat pad (metal)

content.text: Conditioning the clay
Condition
all three colours thoroughly before starting. Cold, under-worked clay will crumble at the cane joins and distort the pattern when reduced.
Building the cane
Roll colour A into a cylinder 8 cm long, 2.5 cm diameter. This is the central core.
Roll colour B into a slab 5 mm thick. Cut six equilateral triangles, each with 3 cm sides. These will pack around the core to form the hexagonal cane.

Roll colour C into a thin slab 2 mm thick. Cut six thin strips 8 cm long, 3 mm wide. Lay one strip along each face of the central cylinder before pressing the triangles against it. The strip creates a thin accent line between core and wedge.

Press one colour-B triangle against the core along a flat face, aligning the triangle so its apex points away from the core. Press it firmly against the core with no air gap. Add the remaining five triangles around the core, one at a time. The assembly should form a regular hexagonal log.
Roll the outer surface of the assembled cane lightly with your palms to compress the joins. The log should be smooth and firm on the outside with no visible gaps at the seams.
Reducing the cane

Reducing makes the pattern smaller and the slices more intricate. Roll the cane on a flat surface under your palms from the centre outward, applying even pressure. Reduce until the cane is 12 cm long and about 1.5 cm in diameter. Work slowly , too much pressure at once distorts the pattern. Trim the distorted ends from the cane with a fettling knife.
Cutting the earring faces
Cut two slices from the cane, each 3 mm thick, using a single clean stroke of the fettling knife. Do not saw , dragging the blade distorts the pattern.
Press each slice gently onto a piece of baking parchment. If the slices are not perfectly round, press lightly from the side to reshape. The slice thickness should be even across the face.
Baking and assembling
Bake the two slices flat on baking parchment at 130°C for 25 minutes. Allow to cool fully before handling.
Apply a coat of acrylic varnish to the front face of each slice. Allow to dry.
Apply jewellery epoxy to the flat pad of each ear stud blank. Press a slice onto each pad and allow the adhesive to cure fully according to the adhesive manufacturer's instructions before wearing.
Variations
Cut thinner slices (1.5 mm) for a more translucent effect if using a lighter clay body.
Attach slices to flat-back resin blanks instead of ear studs for pendants or brooches.
Add a second colour accent line on the outer edge of each triangle by wrapping a thin sheet of clay around the assembled cane before reducing.
Troubleshooter

items.cause: Pressure applied unevenly, or too much pressure at once causing the softer clay colour to move faster than the stiffer colour
items.fix: Reduce more slowly with lighter pressure. Allow the cane to rest for a few minutes between reduction passes if clay is warming up and becoming soft

items.cause: Cane had warmed up during handling; warm polymer clay deforms on cutting
items.fix: Chill the cane in the fridge for 15 minutes before cutting. Always cut with a single downward press, never a sawing motion

items.cause: Triangles were not pressed firmly against the core before reducing
items.fix: Roll the assembled cane under firm palm pressure before reducing to close any gaps. Once baked, gaps cannot be fixed in the same cane, but remaining slices can be used as-is
